message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition.
• Repairs for health and safety issues must be made promptly. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or seek a repair‑and‑deduct remedy (though this is limited in Texas). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice if they intend to re‑rent the unit. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entry notices you receive. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • Report any discriminatory practices to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the legal eviction process: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• Eviction must be filed in court; landlords cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, consider contacting a tenant‑rights group or attorney. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • Texas law allows tenants to deduct repair costs from rent only in very specific circumstances (e.g., landlord fails to fix a major issue after notice). | • Document the issue, send a written notice, and keep receipts. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws. | • Be aware that rent increases must comply with the lease terms and any local ordinances. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities in writing. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed only if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Landlord’s Right to Inspect** | • Landlords may inspect the unit for maintenance or to show it to prospective tenants, but must give reasonable notice. | • Keep a record of inspection notices. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office, Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, local tenant‑rights nonprofits, and HUD. | • Use these resources for disputes or to file complaints. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand rent amount, due dates, security deposit limits, and any special clauses (e.g., pet policy, subletting). 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you in disputes. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 24‑hour notice for entry, 30‑day notice for lease termination, etc. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Send written notices for repairs or maintenance issues. 5. **Keep Copies of All Correspondence** – Emails, letters, and notices should be saved. 6. **Seek Help Early** – If you face eviction or discrimination, contact a tenant‑rights organization or legal aid. --- #### When to Call a Lawyer - You receive an eviction notice and need to contest it. - The landlord refuses to make necessary repairs. - You suspect discrimination or harassment. - You’re unsure about the legality of a lease clause. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is for general educational purposes and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and local ordinances may add additional protections. For personalized guidance, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
